blocks.html:
In the 3D lab you moved unhappy households by hand and watched a city split into red and blue clusters. In this track you write the code that does it.

Every chapter climbs the same ladder: run the book's code, predict what a program prints, reorder scrambled lines, fill blanks, hunt a bug, write a function against checks, then rebuild the chapter's core idea from memory and explain it in words. blocks.html: Almost every model in Think Complexity is a numpy array that changes over time: a row of cells, a grid of sand, a city of households. Three moves cover most of what you need: make an array, look at part of it, and ask a yes/no question of every element at once.

blocks.q: city = np.array([1, 2, 0, 1]). What does np.mean(city == 1) give?

opts.t: 1, because the first house is red
0.5, the fraction of houses that are red
An error: you can't average booleans

blocks.why: city == 1 is [True, False, False, True]. numpy treats True as 1 and False as 0, so the mean is 2/4 = 0.5. "Mean of a mask" = "fraction that satisfy the condition", a pattern you'll use in every chapter.

blocks.solution:
def report(city):
    empty = np.sum(city == 0)
    occupied = city[city != 0]
    frac_red = np.mean(occupied == 1)
    return empty, frac_red

blocks.html:
Here are the rules, exactly as in the 3D city but on one street:

  1. Each house is empty (0), red (1) or blue (2). The street wraps around.
  2. A household looks at the 2r houses around it. It is happy if at least a fraction p of its occupied neighbours share its colour (or if it has no neighbours at all).
  3. Each step, every unhappy household moves to a random empty house.

blocks.html: The book's first chapter describes a set of shifts away from classical, equation-based science. Your street model shows several of them at once: it's discrete (houses, not a smooth density), stochastic (random moves), made of many interacting agents, and studied by computation (you ran it) rather than by analysis (solving for an answer on paper).

blocks.q: Which pair best describes the move from classical models to the Schelling model?

opts.t: From one or two bodies described by equations, to many simple agents studied by simulation

blocks.why: Classical physics models a few bodies with equations you can solve. Schelling's model has hundreds of agents with a simple rule, and the interesting result, strong clustering from mild preferences, appears only when you run it. That is the core shift the book describes.

blocks.q: Nobody in the model wants a segregated street (at p = 0.5 everyone is fine with half their neighbours being different). Yet the street segregates. What is the name for a pattern at the level of the whole system that no individual rule mentions?
blocks.why: Emergence: the system-level property (large single-colour blocks) is not written into any agent's rule. You saw it appear in the plot.

blocks.q: In your own words: why does a city segregate strongly even when each household is happy with half its neighbours being different?
blocks.a:
• A household that moves leaves a gap and lands somewhere new, which changes the neighbourhood of several other households.
  • Moves are local and keep cascading: each move can make a neighbour unhappy, who then moves too.
  • The system only stops when (almost) nobody is unhappy, and the configurations where nobody is unhappy are mostly clustered ones. Mild individual preferences + feedback = strong collective pattern.

blocks.q: Why use np.roll instead of a loop with city[i-1] and city[i+1]?
blocks.a:
• It handles the whole array at once (fast, short code).
  • It wraps around, so the ends of the street need no special case: the street is a ring.
  • np.roll(city, d) lines every house up with its neighbour at offset d, so one comparison checks every house.

blocks.html: A graph is connected if you can get from any node to any other by following edges. The book's algorithm: start somewhere, mark it seen, then keep visiting neighbours of things you've seen until there's nothing new.

blocks.title: reachable_nodes, the book's version
blocks.prompt: Rebuild the search. A stack holds nodes we have found but not processed; seen holds nodes we've processed.

blocks.code:
def reachable_nodes(G, start):
    seen = set()
    stack = [start]
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        if node not in seen:
            seen.add(node)
            stack.extend(G.neighbors(node))
    return seen

G = nx.Graph([(0, 1), (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 5)])
print(sorted(reachable_nodes(G, 2)))
print(sorted(reachable_nodes(G, 5)))
print(len(G), len(reachable_nodes(G, 3)))

blocks.html: Erdős and Rényi found that connectivity doesn't rise smoothly with p. Below a critical value, ER graphs are almost never connected; just above it, they almost always are. For large n the critical value is about **p\* = ln(n) / n**.

blocks.q: Explain how reachable_nodes works, and why it can't loop forever even though the graph has cycles.
blocks.a:
• It keeps a stack of nodes still to process and a set of nodes already processed.
  • Each round it pops a node; if it's new it marks it seen and pushes all its neighbours.
  • Cycles lead back to nodes already in seen, which are popped and skipped, so each node is processed at most once and the loop ends when the stack is empty.
  • The graph is connected exactly when the set it returns contains every node.

blocks.q: What happens to the probability that G(n, p) is connected as p increases, and what's special about ln(n)/n?
blocks.a:
• It stays near 0 for small p, then jumps to near 1 over a narrow range of p: a phase transition.
  • The jump is centred near p\* = ln(n)/n, and it gets sharper as n grows.
  • Intuition: at p\*, the expected number of isolated nodes drops below about one; isolated nodes are the last thing stopping the graph from being connected.

chapters.title: Small world graphs
chapters.tagline: Ring lattices, a few random shortcuts, and why your friends' friends know each other
goals: Build a ring lattice and the Watts–Strogatz graph by rewiring it
Measure clustering (do my friends know each other?) and path length (how many hand-offs?)
Reproduce the small-world result: high clustering and short paths
Write breadth-first search with a deque and use it to find shortest paths

blocks.html:
In 1967 Stanley Milgram asked people in Nebraska to forward a letter to a stranger in Boston, only through people they knew by first name. The letters that arrived took about six hand-offs. That's strange: your friends mostly know each other (a clustered network), and clustered networks usually have long paths, because you keep circling inside your own group.

Watts and Strogatz (1998) explained it with a tiny model: start with a perfectly regular, clustered network, then rewire a few edges at random. This chapter builds that model and measures it.

From the 3D world: in the Village you sent a letter around the lake and then placed a single shortcut. One shortcut cut the trip from many hand-offs to a few. That's the small-world effect, and this chapter measures it. Open the Village

blocks.q: In a network where "my friends mostly know each other", what would you naively expect about the number of hand-offs between two random people?

opts.t: Very few, because everyone is tightly connected
Many, because messages keep circling inside local groups
It can't be estimated without the full network

blocks.why: Local clustering means most of your links lead back into your own neighbourhood, so a purely local network has long paths. Milgram's short chains are the surprise this chapter explains.

blocks.html: A ring lattice puts n nodes in a circle and joins each one to its k nearest neighbours (k/2 on each side). It's the most clustered, most "local" network you can draw.

blocks.code:
def adjacent_edges(nodes, halfk):
    n = len(nodes)
    for i, u in enumerate(nodes):
        for j in range(i + 1, i + halfk + 1):
            v = nodes[j % n]
            yield u, v

def make_ring_lattice(n, k):
    G = nx.Graph()
    nodes = range(n)
    G.add_nodes_from(nodes)
    G.add_edges_from(adjacent_edges(nodes, k // 2))
    return G

lattice = make_ring_lattice(10, 4)
print(lattice.number_of_edges(), "edges")
nx.draw_circular(lattice, with_labels=True, node_color="#c9e9df", node_size=500)
blocks.title: The book's adjacent_edges and make_ring_lattice

blocks.q: A ring lattice has n nodes, each with degree k. How many edges?
blocks.why: Each node has k edge-ends and each edge has two ends, so n·k/2. The generator agrees: each node yields k/2 edges "to the right".

blocks.html: The Watts–Strogatz (WS) graph: go through every edge (u, v); with probability p, keep u but move the other end to a random node that isn't u and isn't already a neighbour of u. At p = 0 you have the lattice; at p = 1 the graph is close to random.

opts.t: Low clustering and short paths (a random graph)
High clustering and long paths (a lattice)

blocks.why: A handful of shortcuts slashes the average path length (each shortcut serves many pairs), while clustering barely moves because almost every local triangle survives. Both properties at once is what Watts and Strogatz meant by small world.

blocks.html:
reachable_nodes from chapter 2 used a stack (last in, first out), so it plunges deep before coming back: depth-first. Swap the stack for a queue (first in, first out) and the search spreads out in rings: first everything one step away, then two steps, and so on. That's breadth-first search (BFS), and it's exactly what you need for shortest paths.

A Python list is slow at removing from the front, so we use collections.deque, which is fast at both ends.

blocks.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque([1, 2])
q.append(3)
q.appendleft(0)
print(q.popleft(), q.pop())
print(list(q))

blocks.q: Explain why a few random shortcuts make paths short but leave clustering high.
blocks.a:
• Path length is a global property: one shortcut between distant parts of the ring gives a fast route to everyone near either end, so the average over all pairs drops a lot.
  • Clustering is local: each shortcut destroys only the few triangles that used the edge it replaced. With p = 0.01, about 99% of edges, and almost all triangles, are untouched.
  • So there's a wide range of p where the network is both clustered (like a lattice) and short (like a random graph): a small world.

blocks.q: What's the one change that turns depth-first search into breadth-first search, and why does BFS give shortest paths?
blocks.a:
• Replace the stack (pop from the end) with a queue (pop from the front, deque.popleft).
  • BFS processes nodes in order of distance: all nodes at distance 1, then 2, and so on. So the first time a node is discovered, it's along a shortest path, and its distance is its parent's + 1.

goals: Compute a degree distribution and its PMF from any graph

blocks.html:
The WS model gets clustering and short paths right. But the book tests it against real data (a Facebook friendship network with about 4,000 people) and finds one thing badly wrong: the degrees. In the WS graph almost everyone has close to k friends. In the real network most people have a few dozen, while a handful have hundreds or thousands. Those people are hubs.

The degree of a node is its number of neighbours. The degree distribution says how many nodes have each degree. This chapter is about distributions with a heavy tail: rare, huge values that matter a lot.

From the 3D world: in the Town you joined as a newcomer and drew lottery tickets, one per existing friendship. The popular got more popular, and towers (hubs) grew. Then you switched popularity off and the towers never formed. Open the Town

sections.title: Heavy tails on a log-log plot

blocks.html: On ordinary axes a heavy tail is invisible: it's a long, flat line near zero. On log-log axes, a power law PMF(k) ∝ k^(−α) becomes a straight line with slope −α. Compare the WS graph with NetworkX's built-in Barabási–Albert graph (which you're about to write yourself).

blocks.title: Two degree distributions, log-log

blocks.q: On log-log axes the BA degree PMF is roughly a straight line. What does that tell you?

opts.t: PMF(k) is roughly proportional to k raised to some negative power
All nodes have the same degree

blocks.why: log PMF = −α log k + c is a straight line on log-log axes, which is the same as PMF(k) ∝ k^(−α): a power law. For the BA model α is about 3.

blocks.html:
Barabási and Albert's idea, which you played as the Town's lottery:

  1. Growth: start with k nodes; add new nodes one at a time.
  2. Preferential attachment: each new node links to k existing nodes, chosen with probability proportional to their degree.

The book's trick for "proportional to degree" is lovely: keep a list, repeated_nodes, where every node appears once per edge it has. Picking uniformly from that list picks nodes in proportion to degree.

blocks.code:
repeated = [0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 2]
counts = {u: repeated.count(u) for u in set(repeated)}
print(counts)
print(round(counts[0] / len(repeated), 3))

blocks.title: _random_subset
blocks.prompt: _random_subset picks k distinct nodes from repeated_nodes. Duplicates must be redrawn, so we loop until the set is big enough. Fill the blanks.
blocks.tests:

assert isinstance(t, set) and len(t) == 3, f"Expected a set of 3 distinct nodes, got {t}"
assert t <= {0, 1, 2, 3}, "Targets must come from the list"

assert 0.6 < hits < 0.73, f"Node 0 is 8 of 12 entries, so it should be picked about 2/3 of the time; got {hits:.2f}"

blocks.title: barabasi_albert_graph
blocks.prompt:
Write the book's barabasi_albert_graph(n, k). Start with k nodes and no edges; the first targets are those k nodes. For each new source from k to n-1:

  1. link source to every target,
  2. add the targets and source (k times each) to repeated_nodes,
  3. choose the next targets with _random_subset(repeated_nodes, k).
blocks.tests:

assert G.number_of_edges() == 3 * (500 - 3), f"Each new node adds k edges: expected {3*497}, got {G.number_of_edges()}"

hints: zip([source] * k, targets) makes the k edges from the new node.
After adding edges, repeated_nodes.extend(targets) and repeated_nodes.extend([source] * k): every new edge adds one entry for each end.
blocks.starter:
def barabasi_albert_graph(n, k):

    # your loop here

blocks.solution:
def barabasi_albert_graph(n, k):
    G = nx.empty_graph(k)
    targets = list(range(k))
    repeated_nodes = []
    for source in range(k, n):
        G.add_edges_from(zip([source] * k, targets))
        repeated_nodes.extend(targets)
        repeated_nodes.extend([source] * k)
        targets = _random_subset(repeated_nodes, k)
    return G

sections.title: The CCDF: a cleaner view of the tail

blocks.html: PMFs of real data are noisy in the tail (most high degrees appear once or not at all). The book prefers the complementary CDF: CCDF(x) = the fraction of values greater than x. For a power law it's also a straight line on log-log axes, and it's much smoother.

blocks.title: ccdf
blocks.prompt: Write ccdf(values, xs) returning a numpy array with, for each x in xs, the fraction of values that are strictly greater than x.
blocks.tests:

assert c.tolist() == [1.0, 0.75, 0.25, 0.0], f"Expected [1.0, 0.75, 0.25, 0.0], got {c.tolist()}"
assert len(ccdf([5, 5], range(10))) == 10, "One result per x"
hints: "Mean of a mask" again: np.mean(values > x) is the fraction above x.

blocks.code:
def ccdf(values, xs):
    values = np.asarray(values)
    return np.array([np.mean(values > x) for x in xs])

ws = nx.watts_strogatz_graph(3000, 10, 0.05, seed=2)
ba = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(3000, 5, seed=2)
xs = np.arange(1, 300)
for name, G in [("WS", ws), ("BA", ba)]:
    d = [G.degree(u) for u in G]
    plt.plot(xs, ccdf(d, xs), label=name)
plt.xscale("log"); plt.yscale("log"); plt.ylim(1e-4, 1.5)
plt.xlabel("degree x"); plt.ylabel("fraction with degree > x"); plt.legend()

blocks.q: In the CCDF plot, the WS curve plunges to zero just past x ≈ 15, while BA's declines in a straight line out to the hundreds. In plain words?

opts.t: Both graphs have hubs, BA's are just bigger
In WS nobody has many more friends than average; in BA a few nodes have tens of times the average
WS has more edges than BA
The CCDF can't compare graphs with different k

blocks.why: WS degrees are concentrated near the mean, so the CCDF drops off a cliff. BA's power-law tail means the chance of finding a node with degree above x falls slowly, so hubs exist.

blocks.q: Why does the BA model produce hubs while the WS model doesn't? Mention both ingredients.
blocks.a:
• WS starts from a lattice where every node has degree k and rewires a few edges, so degrees stay close to k.
  • BA has growth (old nodes have had more time to collect links) and preferential attachment (high-degree nodes are more likely to get the next link).
  • Together they create a feedback loop: being big makes you grow faster. The result is a power-law degree distribution with a few huge hubs.
  • Remove preferential attachment (uniform choice) and the tail becomes exponential: no hubs.

blocks.q: What does the repeated_nodes list contain, and why does choosing from it uniformly implement preferential attachment?
blocks.a:
• Every node appears in the list once for each edge it has (both ends of every edge get added).
  • So a node with degree d occupies d slots, and a uniform random pick lands on it with probability d / (total degree): proportional to degree.
  • It avoids computing probabilities explicitly; updating the list is just extend.

chapters.title: Cellular automata
chapters.tagline: A row of cells, eight-entry rule tables, and the strange worlds of rules 30 and 110
goals: Turn a rule number like 30 into its rule table with binary
Compute a whole new row at once with np.correlate and a window of [4, 2, 1]
Run any elementary CA and sort its behaviour into Wolfram's four classes
Use Rule 30's centre column as a pseudo-random bit generator
chapters.prelude:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

blocks.html:
A cellular automaton (CA) is a world reduced to the bare minimum:

  • cells in a row (or grid),
  • each in one of a few states (here 0 or 1),
  • a rule that gives a cell's next state from its own state and its neighbours',
  • discrete time: every cell updates at once, step after step.

Wolfram's elementary CAs use a 1-D row and look at three cells: left, self, right. Three cells of 0/1 give 2³ = 8 possible neighbourhoods, so a rule is just a table of 8 output bits. Read those 8 bits as a binary number and you get the rule's name: Rule 0 to Rule 255.

From the 3D world: in Automata you predicted the next row by hand, wrote your own rule table, and sorted rules 0, 18, 30 and 110 into classes. Here you make the computer do the same work. Open Automata

blocks.q: How many different elementary CA rules are there?
blocks.why: Each of the 8 neighbourhoods can map to 0 or 1, so there are 2⁸ = 256 rule tables, named Rule 0 to Rule 255.

sections.title: From a rule number to a rule table

blocks.html: The book's trick: neighbourhood (left, self, right) is itself a 3-bit binary number, 4·left + 2·self + 1·right, from 0 to 7. Write the rule number in binary, and bit v of the rule is the output for neighbourhood v.

blocks.code:
rule = 50
bits = [(rule >> v) & 1 for v in range(8)]
print(bits)
print(format(rule, "08b"))

blocks.title: make_table
blocks.prompt: Write make_table(rule) returning a numpy array table of length 8 where table[v] is the output for neighbourhood number v. The book uses np.unpackbits, which gives the most significant bit first, so it reverses the result. Any method is fine.
blocks.tests:
assert list(make_table(50)) == [0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0], f"Rule 50 should be [0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0], got {list(make_table(50))}"
assert list(make_table(0)) == [0] * 8, "Rule 0 maps everything to 0"
assert list(make_table(255)) == [1] * 8, "Rule 255 maps everything to 1"
assert make_table(30)[4] == 1 and make_table(30)[7] == 0, "Rule 30: 100 -> 1, 111 -> 0"
hints: np.unpackbits(np.array([rule], dtype=np.uint8)) gives 8 bits, most significant first. [::-1] reverses them.
blocks.starter:
def make_table(rule):
    pass
blocks.solution:
def make_table(rule):
    rule = np.array([rule], dtype=np.uint8)
    table = np.unpackbits(rule)[::-1]
    return table

blocks.html: To get the next row you need, for every cell, 4·left + 2·self + 1·right. np.correlate slides a window along the row and does exactly that sum at every position (the ends are padded with 0).

blocks.code:
row = np.array([0, 1, 1, 0, 1])
print(np.correlate(row, [4, 2, 1], mode="same"))

blocks.html: Read the output position by position. The middle cell (index 2) sees left=1, self=1, right=0, so 4 + 2 + 0 = 6. Then the next state is just table[6]. Indexing a table with an array looks up every cell at once.

blocks.title: step
blocks.prompt: Fill the blanks in step(array, i, table), which computes row i of a 2-D array from row i-1.

assert a[1].tolist() == [0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0], f"Rule 50 from a single cell: expected [0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0], got {a[1].tolist()}"

blocks.title: Rules 50, 30 and 110

blocks.html: Change the rules. Try 18, 90, 54, 73, 184.

Wolfram sorted the 256 rules by what they do from a random start:

ClassBehaviourExample
1Everything dies out to a uniform stateRule 0
2Simple, stable or repeating structuresRule 50
3Chaotic, random-looking foreverRule 30
4Localised structures that move and interact: neither order nor chaosRule 110

Rule 110 is Turing complete: with the right starting row it can compute anything a computer can. Simple rules, universal computation.

blocks.q: You run a rule from a random start and see triangles of all sizes, never settling, with no repeating pattern. Which class?
blocks.why: Endless random-looking structure is Class 3, like Rule 30. Class 4 would show persistent "particles" moving through a regular background and colliding.

blocks.q: What's surprising about Rule 30, given how it's built?

opts.t: It needs a random number generator to run
It's completely deterministic, yet its output passes many tests of randomness
It only works on wide rows
It produces a different picture each time from the same start

blocks.why: Rule 30 has no randomness in it at all, yet from a single cell its centre column looks like coin flips. Mathematica used it as its random-number generator for years.

blocks.title: Rebuild run_ca
blocks.prompt: From memory: run_ca(rule, n_rows, width) returns an (n_rows, width) uint8 array whose first row has a single 1 in the middle (width // 2) and whose later rows follow the rule.
blocks.tests:
a = run_ca(90, 4, 9)
assert a.shape == (4, 9), f"Shape should be (4, 9), got {a.shape}"
assert a[3].tolist() == [0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0], f"Rule 90 row 3 is a Sierpinski row [0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1,0], got {a[3].tolist()}"
assert run_ca(0, 3, 5)[1:].sum() == 0, "Rule 0 kills everything after the first row"
blocks.starter:
def run_ca(rule, n_rows, width):
    pass
blocks.solution:
def run_ca(rule, n_rows, width):
    table = np.unpackbits(np.array([rule], dtype=np.uint8))[::-1]
    array = np.zeros((n_rows, width), dtype=np.uint8)
    array[0, width // 2] = 1
    for i in range(1, n_rows):
        c = np.correlate(array[i - 1], [4, 2, 1], mode="same")
        array[i] = table[c]
    return array

blocks.q: Walk through how one row of an elementary CA is computed with numpy, from rule number to new row.
blocks.a:
• Turn the rule number into an 8-entry table: bit v of the rule is the output for neighbourhood v.
  • For every cell, encode its neighbourhood as one number: 4·left + 2·self + 1·right. np.correlate(row, [4, 2, 1], mode="same") does this for the whole row.
  • Look up all cells at once: new_row = table[codes].

blocks.q: What are Wolfram's four classes, and why is Class 4 the interesting one?
blocks.a:
• 1: dies to uniform; 2: simple stable/periodic patterns; 3: chaos (random-looking); 4: complex localised structures that move and interact.
  • Class 4 sits between order and chaos. Structures persist long enough to carry information and interact to process it, which is why Rule 110 can perform universal computation.

chapters.title: Game of Life
chapters.tagline: Two rules on a grid, gliders that walk, and a gun that broke a conjecture
goals: State Conway's rules and apply them to any cell by hand
Count all 8 neighbours of every cell at once with np.roll
Use the book's kernel-10 trick to turn "alive + neighbours" into one lookup
Explain what gliders, oscillators and the glider gun show about emergence

blocks.html:
Conway's Game of Life (1970) is a 2-D cellular automaton. Every cell is alive or dead and has 8 neighbours (including diagonals). Each step, all cells update at once:

  • Birth: a dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbours comes alive.
  • Survival: a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours stays alive.
  • Everyone else dies or stays dead (from loneliness or overcrowding).

That's all. From these two rules come still lifes, blinking oscillators, spaceships that glide across the grid, and machines that build other machines.
From the 3D world: in Life you predicted births and deaths, built a glider by hand, and fired the glider gun. Now you'll write the engine that runs it. Open Life

blocks.q: A live cell has 4 live neighbours. A dead cell has 2. What happens to each?

opts.t: The live cell dies (overcrowding); the dead cell stays dead
The live cell survives; the dead cell comes alive

blocks.why: Survival needs 2 or 3 neighbours, so 4 is too many. Birth needs exactly 3, so 2 is not enough.

sections.title: The book's trick: weight yourself by 10

blocks.html: The book counts neighbours with scipy.signal.correlate2d and a 3×3 kernel whose centre is 10 instead of 0. Then every cell gets one number: c = 10 × (alive?) + neighbours. A dead cell with 3 neighbours has c = 3; a live cell with 2 or 3 has c = 12 or 13. So the whole rule is: alive next iff c is 3, 12 or 13.

blocks.code:
from scipy.signal import correlate2d

kernel = np.array([[1, 1, 1],
                   [1, 10, 1],
                   [1, 1, 1]])

def step(a):
    c = correlate2d(a, kernel, mode="same", boundary="wrap")
    return ((c == 3) | (c == 12) | (c == 13)).astype(np.uint8)

a = np.zeros((6, 6), dtype=np.uint8)
a[2, 1:4] = 1
print(correlate2d(a, kernel, mode="same", boundary="wrap"))
print(step(a))

blocks.title: The Gosper glider gun

blocks.html:
The book uses Life for a philosophical point. Gliders "exist" at a higher level of description than cells. Are they real things, or just a convenient way to talk about cell patterns?

  • Realism: higher-level entities like gliders (or species, or economies) are real and the theories about them are true or false.
  • Instrumentalism: they're useful models; a theory is judged by how well it predicts, not whether it's "true".

Life also shows that simple rules can be universal: you can build logic gates from gliders, and Life is Turing complete.

blocks.q: Someone says: "Gliders aren't real. There are only cells turning on and off." Which point does the book make in reply?

opts.t: They're right; higher-level descriptions are errors
"Glider" is a valid, useful higher-level description, and the debate over whether it's "real" is the realism vs instrumentalism question
Gliders are real because they're in the source code
The rules of Life explicitly define gliders

blocks.why: Nothing in the two rules mentions gliders, yet "a glider moves one cell diagonally every 4 steps" predicts the system perfectly. Whether such emergent objects are "real" is exactly what realists and instrumentalists disagree about.

blocks.q: Explain the kernel-10 trick: why is "alive next step" the same as "c is 3, 12 or 13"?
blocks.a:
• The kernel adds up the 8 neighbours with weight 1 and the cell itself with weight 10, so c = 10·self + neighbours.
  • Dead cells have c = 0…8; live cells have c = 10…18. The two ranges can't overlap.
  • Birth (dead, 3 neighbours) → 3. Survival (alive, 2 or 3) → 12 or 13. Any other value means dead next step.

blocks.q: What did the glider gun prove, and why does it matter for complexity science?
blocks.a:
• Conway conjectured that every finite starting pattern eventually stops growing. The gun is a finite pattern whose population grows forever (one glider every 30 steps), so the conjecture is false.
  • It shows you often can't predict what simple rules will do by reasoning about them: you have to run them. And guns are a building block for computation in Life (glider streams as signals).

chapters.title: Physical modeling
chapters.tagline: Ink that spreads, chemicals that make spots, water that finds a way through rock
goals: Model diffusion with the discrete Laplacian
Run a reaction–diffusion system and see Turing patterns emerge
Write a percolation model and find its critical porosity near 0.593
Estimate a fractal dimension from a log-log slope

blocks.html:
Ink in water spreads because molecules jiggle randomly. On a grid, that becomes a simple rule: each step, every cell moves a little toward the average of its neighbours. The amount a cell differs from its neighbours is the Laplacian:

Δa = (up + down + left + right) − 4·a

and the update is a ← a + r·Δa for a small rate r. High spots fall, low spots rise, and everything smooths out.
From the 3D world: in Rock & ink you drilled through rock and grew Turing spots. The spots are the reaction–diffusion model here; the drilling is percolation. Open Rock & ink

blocks.html:
In 1952 Alan Turing proposed that two chemicals that react and diffuse at different speeds can form stable patterns: spots and stripes, like a leopard's coat. The book uses the Gray–Scott model with chemicals A and B:

  • A is fed in at rate f; B is removed at rate k;
  • the reaction A + 2B → 3B turns A into B where B already is;
  • A diffuses faster than B.

blocks.code:
def gray_scott(f, k, n=100, steps=5000):
    A = np.ones((n, n))
    B = np.zeros((n, n))
    A[40:60, 40:60] = 0.5           # a square seed in the middle
    B[40:60, 40:60] = 0.25
    B += 0.02 * np.random.default_rng(0).random((n, n))
    ra, rb = 0.16, 0.08             # A diffuses twice as fast as B
    for _ in range(steps):
        reaction = A * B * B
        A += ra * laplacian(A) - reaction + f * (1 - A)
        B += rb * laplacian(B) + reaction - (f + k) * B
    return B

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.4))
for ax, (f, k) in zip(axes, [(0.035, 0.065), (0.040, 0.060), (0.025, 0.055)]):
    ax.imshow(gray_scott(f, k), cmap="magma", interpolation="bicubic")
    ax.set_title(f"f={f}, k={k}"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])

sections.title: Percolation: can the water get through?

blocks.html: Make an n×n grid of rock. Each cell is porous with probability q, otherwise solid. Pour water on the top row. Water spreads from wet cells to porous neighbours (up, down, left, right; no wrapping this time: the top and bottom are real edges). If water ever reaches the bottom row, the rock percolates.

blocks.title: spread one step
blocks.prompt: Write spread(wet, porous): return the new boolean wet array after one step. A cell is wet next step if it's porous and it's already wet or one of its 4 neighbours is wet. Use slicing, not np.roll, so nothing wraps around the edges.
blocks.tests:
porous = np.ones((3, 3), dtype=bool); porous[1, 0] = False
wet = np.zeros((3, 3), dtype=bool); wet[0, :] = True
w1 = spread(wet, porous)
assert w1[1].tolist() == [False, True, True], f"Row 1 should become [False, True, True] (cell (1,0) is solid), got {w1[1].tolist()}"
assert not w1[2].any(), "Water moves one cell per step"
col = np.zeros((4, 4), dtype=bool); col[:, 0] = True
w = np.zeros((4, 4), dtype=bool); w[3, 3] = True
assert not spread(w, col)[0, 3] and not spread(w, col)[3, 0], "No wrapping: water can't jump from one edge to the other"
hints: nb[1:, :] |= wet[:-1, :] marks every cell whose upper neighbour is wet. Write the same for below, left and right.
blocks.solution:
def spread(wet, porous):
    nb = np.zeros_like(wet)
    nb[1:, :] |= wet[:-1, :]
    nb[:-1, :] |= wet[1:, :]
    nb[:, 1:] |= wet[:, :-1]
    nb[:, :-1] |= wet[:, 1:]
    return porous & (wet | nb)

blocks.title: Probability of percolating vs porosity

blocks.q: The jump from "almost never" to "almost always" percolating is centred near q ≈ 0.593 and gets sharper for bigger grids. Where have you seen this shape before?

opts.t: The connectivity of Erdős–Rényi graphs in chapter 2
The degree distribution of BA graphs

blocks.why: Both are phase transitions: a global property (connected graph / percolating rock) switches on abruptly at a critical value of a local probability. The book's Map of Ideas links them for this reason.

blocks.html:
At q = q_c, the wet cluster is a fractal: full of holes at every scale. One way to see it: how does the number of wet cells grow with grid size n? A solid square grows like n²; a line like n¹. The percolating cluster grows like n^D with D ≈ 1.85, a dimension between a line and a plane.

To estimate D, plot log(cells) against log(n): the slope is D.

blocks.code:

counts = 3 * sizes ** 2
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(np.log(sizes), np.log(counts), 1)
print(round(slope, 3))

blocks.code:
def wet_count(n, q, rng):
    porous = rng.random((n, n)) < q
    wet = np.zeros_like(porous); wet[0] = porous[0]
    while True:
        new = spread(wet, porous)
        if (new == wet).all():
            return wet.sum(), wet[-1].any()
        wet = new

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
sizes, counts = [], []
for n in [20, 40, 60, 80]:
    got = [c for c, perc in (wet_count(n, 0.593, rng) for _ in range(40)) if perc]
    sizes.append(n); counts.append(np.mean(got))
D = np.polyfit(np.log(sizes), np.log(counts), 1)[0]
print("estimated fractal dimension:", round(D, 2), "(theory: about 1.9 for big grids)")
plt.loglog(sizes, counts, "o-", label="wet cells (percolating runs)")
plt.loglog(sizes, np.array(sizes) ** 2 * counts[0] / sizes[0] ** 2, "--", label="slope 2 (filled)")
plt.xlabel("n"); plt.ylabel("cells"); plt.legend()

blocks.q: Describe the percolation model and what "critical porosity" means.
blocks.a:
• An n×n grid; each cell porous with probability q. Water starts in the top row and repeatedly spreads to porous neighbours.
  • The rock percolates if water reaches the bottom row.
  • Below about q = 0.593 large grids almost never percolate; above it they almost always do. That threshold is the critical value of a phase transition, and the transition gets sharper as n grows.

blocks.q: What does a fractal dimension of about 1.85 mean for the wet cluster, and how do you measure it?
blocks.a:
• The number of wet cells grows like n^1.85 as the grid grows: faster than a line (n¹), slower than a filled square (n²). The cluster has holes at every scale.
  • Measure it by counting cells for several sizes and fitting a straight line to log(count) vs log(n); the slope is the dimension.
